records.source: Πᾶς γὰρ ἀρχιερεὺς ἐξ ἀνθρώπων λαμβανόμενος ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων καθίσταται τὰ πρὸς τὸν θεόν, ἵνα προσφέρῃ δῶρά τε καὶ θυσίας ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν, μετριοπαθεῖν δυνάμενος τοῖς ἀγνοοῦσι καὶ πλανωμένοις ἐπεὶ καὶ αὐτὸς περίκειται ἀσθένειαν, καὶ δι’ αὐτὴν ὀφείλει, καθὼς περὶ τοῦ λαοῦ, οὕτως καὶ περὶ αὑτοῦ προσφέρειν περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν.
records.gloss: Every for high priest from men being taken on behalf of men is appointed [in] the [things] toward the God, that he may offer gifts both and sacrifices for sins, \v 2 to deal moderately being able with the [ones] being ignorant and going astray, since also he himself is surrounded [with] weakness, \v 3 and because of it he ought, as for the people, so also for himself to offer for sins.
pieces: Every high priest is taken from among {{gender:human beings|men}} and put in office on behalf of {{gender:human beings|men}} to deal with what concerns God: he brings gifts and sacrifices for sins.
He is able to be gentle and restrained with those who sin in ignorance and wander from the way, since weakness clings to him as well.
That weakness is why he must bring offerings for sins on his own account, just as he does for the people.

L.1: For every high priest, being taken from among {{gender:human beings|men}}, is appointed on behalf of {{gender:human beings|men}} [in] the things toward God, so that he may offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins,
L.2: being able to deal moderately with those who are ignorant and going astray, since he himself also is surrounded with weakness;
L.3: and because of it he is obliged, as for the people, so also for himself, to offer for sins.

R.1: Every high priest is chosen from among human beings. He is put in that place to serve people in the things that have to do with God. He offers gifts and sacrifices for sins.
R.2: He can be gentle with people who do wrong because they do not know better, or because they have wandered off the right path. He can be gentle because he is weak too.
R.3: And because he is weak, he has to offer sacrifices for his own sins, just as he does for the sins of the people.

decisions.choice: the high priest of Israel, whose task was to offer sacrifices on the people's behalf
decisions.reason: The author describes the high priesthood set up in the law (Exodus 28-29; Leviticus 8-9; Leviticus 16), and uses it to explain Jesus as high priest (4:14-16). "Gifts and sacrifices" covers the offerings in general; 8:3 uses the same pair. The point is that a high priest is himself human and acts for human beings.

decisions.choice: deal moderately: keep one's feelings in measure, neither harsh nor indulgent
decisions.reason: μετριοπαθεῖν means to hold one's feelings within bounds. With wrongdoers it means not flaring up in anger and not excusing the wrong either. It is a different word from the one in 4:15, where Jesus is able to "sympathize" with our weaknesses.

decisions.choice: the ignorant and wandering: people who sin without meaning to defy God
decisions.reason: The law provided sacrifices for sins done in ignorance or by straying (Leviticus 4:2, 13, 22, 27; Numbers 15:22-29), but not for sin done "with a high hand", in open defiance (Numbers 15:30-31). The author has this distinction in view; it returns in 10:26.

decisions.choice: the high priest's offering for his own sins: Leviticus 9:7; 16:6, 11
decisions.reason: On the Day of Atonement the high priest first offered a bull for his own sin and his household's, and then the offering for the people (Leviticus 16:6, 11, 15; compare 9:7). Hebrews 7:27 comes back to this: Jesus had no need to do so.

decisions.choice: {{gender:human beings|men}}
decisions.reason: The point is that the high priest shares the nature of those he serves, human beings, men and women alike, so the gender setting applies; "men" is the traditional alternative. Readable says "human beings" and "people", which need no setting.

decisions.choice: weakness clings to him
decisions.reason: περίκειται means to have something lying around one, like a garment or a chain (Acts 28:20 uses it of Paul's chain). "Clings to him" keeps the picture of weakness he cannot take off.

records.source: καὶ οὐχ ἑαυτῷ τις λαμβάνει τὴν τιμήν, ἀλλὰ καλούμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ, καθώσπερ καὶ Ἀαρών.
records.gloss: And not to himself anyone takes the honor, but being called by the God, just as also Aaron.
pieces: Nobody seizes this honor for himself; it belongs to the one God calls, as God called Aaron.

L.4: And no one takes the honor for himself, but [he receives it] being called by God, just as Aaron also [was].

R.4: No one can give this honor to himself. God has to call him to it, as God called Aaron.

decisions.choice: the honor: the high priestly office itself
decisions.reason: τιμήν is the honor of holding the office. The next verse picks up the thought with the verb "glorify": Christ did not give himself this honor either.

decisions.choice: Aaron was appointed by God, and those who claimed the priesthood for themselves were judged
decisions.reason: God chose Aaron and his sons (Exodus 28:1). When Korah and his followers claimed the priesthood, they were judged, and Aaron's staff that budded showed God's choice (Numbers 16-17). King Uzziah was struck with skin disease when he burned incense in the temple (2 Chronicles 26:16-21).

decisions.choice: it belongs to the one God calls, as God called Aaron
alternatives: he receives it when God calls him
decisions.reason: The Greek leaves the verb of the second half unstated ("but being called by God"). Balanced and Readable supply it and repeat "God" so the comparison with Aaron is clear.

records.source: Οὕτως καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς οὐχ ἑαυτὸν ἐδόξασεν γενηθῆναι ἀρχιερέα, ἀλλ’ ὁ λαλήσας πρὸς αὐτόν· Υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε·
records.gloss: So also the Christ not himself glorified to become high priest, but the [one] having spoken to him: Son of me are you, I today have begotten you.
pieces: In the same way {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} did not give {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} the glory of becoming high priest. That glory came from the one who said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "You are {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} Son; today I have fathered {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."

L.5: So also the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} did not glorify {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} to become high priest, but the one who spoke to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} [glorified {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}]: "You are {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} Son; I today have begotten {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."

R.5: In the same way, {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} did not take for {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} the glory of being high priest. God gave it to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. God said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "You are {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} Son. Today I have fathered {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."

decisions.choice: Psalm 2:7
decisions.reason: The words are Psalm 2:7, already quoted in 1:5. In the psalm God speaks them to the king he has installed on Zion. The author reads them as God's words to the Son, and here sets them beside Psalm 110:4 (verse 6): the one God calls Son is the one God appoints priest. The Greek of the line follows the Hebrew closely.

decisions.choice: today: the day of the Son's appointment, which the author does not date
alternatives: the Son's eternal relationship to the Father
decisions.reason: In the psalm "today" is the king's coronation day. The author does not say which day he has in mind. Hebrews links the Son's appointment with his being raised and seated at God's right hand (1:3-5; 5:9-10; 7:28), and Acts 13:33 applies the same verse to the resurrection, but the text here does not settle it.

decisions.choice: but [he was glorified by] the one who spoke to him
alternatives: but the one who spoke to him [said]
decisions.reason: The second half has no verb of its own; "glorified" carries over from the first half. God, who spoke Psalm 2:7 to him, is the one who gave him the honor. ἐδόξασεν picks up "the honor" of verse 4.

decisions.choice: fathered
decisions.reason: γεγέννηκά is the ordinary verb for a father having a child. Literal keeps the traditional "begotten"; Balanced and Readable use the plainer "fathered". The verb describes the relationship God declares, not a physical birth (see the meaning decision on "today").

decisions.choice: God gave it to him. God said to him
decisions.reason: Readable names God, whom the Greek calls only "the one who spoke to him", and states the gift that the Greek implies.

records.source: καθὼς καὶ ἐν ἑτέρῳ λέγει· Σὺ ἱερεὺς εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισέδεκ, ὃς ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ δεήσεις τε καὶ ἱκετηρίας πρὸς τὸν δυνάμενον σῴζειν αὐτὸν ἐκ θανάτου μετὰ κραυγῆς ἰσχυρᾶς καὶ δακρύων προσενέγκας καὶ εἰσακουσθεὶς ἀπὸ τῆς εὐλαβείας, καίπερ ὢν υἱός, ἔμαθεν ἀφ’ ὧν ἔπαθεν τὴν ὑπακοήν, καὶ τελειωθεὶς ἐγένετο πᾶσιν τοῖς ὑπακούουσιν αὐτῷ αἴτιος σωτηρίας αἰωνίου, προσαγορευθεὶς ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀρχιερεὺς κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισέδεκ.
records.gloss: as also in another he says: You [are] priest to the age according to the order Melchizedek, \v 7 who in the days of the flesh of him prayers both and supplications to the [one] being able to save him out of death with crying strong and tears having offered and having been heard from the reverence, \v 8 although being son, he learned from [the things] which he suffered the obedience, \v 9 and having been perfected he became to all those obeying him cause of salvation eternal, \v 10 having been designated by the God high priest according to the order Melchizedek.
pieces: As {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} also says in another place, "You are a priest forever, of the order of Melchizedek."

In the days of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} life in the flesh, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} offered up prayers and pleas, crying aloud and weeping, to the one who was able to save {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} out of death, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was heard for {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} godly fear.
Even though {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was a Son, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} learned obedience by the things {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} suffered.
And having been made perfect, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} became the cause of eternal salvation for everyone who obeys {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}},
for God declared {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} a high priest of the order of Melchizedek.

L.6: As also in another [place] {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says, "You [are] a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek."
L.7: [It was {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}] who, in the days of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} flesh, having offered up both prayers and supplications with loud crying and tears to the one who was able to save {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} out of death, and having been heard because of [{{deity_pronoun:his|His}}] reverence,
L.8: although being a Son, learned obedience from the things which {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} suffered;
L.9: and having been made perfect, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} became to all those who obey {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} [the] cause of eternal salvation,
L.10: having been designated by God a high priest according to the order of Melchizedek.

R.6: And in another place God says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "You are a priest forever, the kind of priest Melchizedek was."
R.7: When Jesus lived on earth as a human being, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} cried out loudly to God with tears. He prayed and pleaded with the one who could save {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} out of death. And God heard {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, because {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} honored God with deep respect.
R.8: He was God's Son, and yet {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} learned what it is to obey through the things {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} suffered.
R.9: When {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had been made complete, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} became the one who brings eternal salvation to all who obey {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.
R.10: God named {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} a high priest, the kind of priest Melchizedek was.

decisions.choice: Psalm 110:4 (109:4 Greek)
decisions.reason: The line is Psalm 110:4, from the psalm whose first verse the author quoted in 1:13. "In another [place]" means another psalm: the speaker is still God, who spoke Psalm 2:7 in verse 5. In the psalm the line is introduced as an oath ("the LORD has sworn and will not change his mind"); the author quotes that part in 7:21. The Greek follows the Hebrew closely. Melchizedek appears in Genesis 14:18-20 as king of Salem and priest of God Most High; chapter 7 explains what the comparison means.

decisions.choice: according to the order of Melchizedek: a priest of the same kind or rank as Melchizedek
decisions.reason: τάξιν means an order, rank or arrangement. It does not mean descent: 7:3 stresses that Melchizedek has no recorded ancestry, and 7:15 restates the phrase as "in the likeness of Melchizedek". The priest of the psalm is a priest like Melchizedek, not one of Aaron's line.

decisions.choice: the days of his flesh: his mortal human life
alternatives: the days when he was subject to sinful desires
decisions.reason: Here "flesh" means human life in its frailty and mortality, as in 2:14 ("blood and flesh"). It says nothing of sin; 4:15 says he was without sin.

decisions.choice: prayers with loud cries and tears: the Gospels' account of Gethsemane, and perhaps the cross
alternatives: a general description of his life of prayer
decisions.reason: Prayer to the one able to save him from death recalls Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane that the cup might pass from him (Matthew 26:36-46; Mark 14:32-42; Luke 22:39-46). The Gospels do not mention tears there, and the loud cry fits the cross (Mark 15:34, 37), so the author may have the whole passion in view. The language also echoes the psalms of the righteous sufferer who cries to God (Psalm 22:2-3, 25). The author names no scene.

decisions.choice: he was heard because of his reverence; God answered by bringing him out of death, not by sparing him from dying
alternatives: he was heard and set free from his fear
he was heard and spared from dying
decisions.reason: ἀπὸ with εὐλαβείας most naturally gives the reason he was heard: his reverent submission to God (the same noun family in 12:28 for worship "with reverence and awe"). Some take it as "heard [and delivered] from his fear", but the noun elsewhere means devout reverence, not terror. Jesus still died, so the answer is that God brought him out of death (the Greek preposition is ἐκ, "out of"), raising him (13:20). The translation keeps "save him out of death" at every level.

decisions.choice: he learned obedience: he came to know by experience what obedience to God costs
alternatives: he moved from disobedience to obedience
decisions.reason: The Greek plays on two similar verbs, ἔμαθεν ("he learned") and ἔπαθεν ("he suffered"). It does not imply he had been disobedient: 4:15 says he was without sin. Even though he was the Son, who might have been expected to be spared, he obeyed the Father through suffering and so learned obedience by doing it (compare Philippians 2:8; 10:5-10).

decisions.choice: made perfect: brought to the goal, fully fitted for his office as Savior and high priest
decisions.reason: As at 2:10, τελειόω means to bring something to completion. Through suffering, death and exaltation, the Son was made fully what he was appointed to be, the high priest who saves. It is not moral improvement; he was always without sin (4:15; 7:26-28).

decisions.choice: cause of eternal salvation: the one through whom it comes about
decisions.reason: αἴτιος means the one responsible for something, its cause. Compare 2:10, where he is the "pioneer" of salvation. "Eternal" contrasts this salvation with the repeated, temporary results of the old sacrifices (9:12, 9:15).

decisions.choice: having been designated: God addressed him as high priest, in the words of Psalm 110:4
alternatives: after he had become high priest he was called so
decisions.reason: προσαγορευθεὶς means to address someone by a title or to name them publicly. The participle explains verse 9: he is the cause of eternal salvation as the high priest whom God declared him to be. The verse repeats Psalm 110:4 and leads back to it in 6:20 and chapter 7.

decisions.choice: of the order of Melchizedek (Balanced); the kind of priest Melchizedek was (Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "according to the order of". Balanced says "of the order of", which reads naturally. Readable states the sense (a priest of the same kind), since "order" in this sense is unfamiliar and "line" would suggest descent.

decisions.choice: godly fear
decisions.reason: εὐλαβείας is the awe and devotion of someone who fears God. "Godly fear" says that in two plain words; Literal has "reverence".

decisions.choice: God says ... When Jesus lived ... God heard him ... God's Son
decisions.reason: Readable names Jesus and God where the Greek uses "who", "he" and "the one who was able", and turns the passive "he was heard" into "God heard him", since the long Greek sentence is broken into short ones.

decisions.choice: made complete
decisions.reason: Readable says "made complete" for τελειόω (Literal and Balanced: "made perfect"), because "perfect" can sound as if he had faults that needed fixing. See the meaning decision on the word.

decisions.choice: he learned what it is to obey
decisions.reason: Readable spells out "learned obedience" in plain words; it means he learned by experience what obeying God involves.

records.source: Περὶ οὗ πολὺς ἡμῖν ὁ λόγος καὶ δυσερμήνευτος λέγειν, ἐπεὶ νωθροὶ γεγόνατε ταῖς ἀκοαῖς·
records.gloss: Concerning which much for us the word and hard-to-explain to say, since sluggish you have become in the hearings.
pieces: About this we have a great deal to say, and it is hard to put into words, because you have become sluggish listeners.

L.11: Concerning which our message [is] long and hard to explain in the telling, since you have become sluggish in [your] ears.

R.11: We have a lot to say about this, but it is hard to explain to you, because you have become lazy about listening.

decisions.choice: concerning this: the subject of Christ's priesthood like Melchizedek's
decisions.reason: οὗ can be "which" (a subject) or "whom" (a person). Either way the topic is the one just named, a high priest of the order of Melchizedek, which the author takes up in chapter 7 after this warning.

decisions.choice: we: the author speaking of himself and his teaching
alternatives: the author and the readers together
decisions.reason: Here "we" stands over against "you" (the readers), so it is the author's own voice, as again in 6:9 and 6:11. Elsewhere in Hebrews "we" usually includes the readers (2:1, 4:14).

decisions.choice: you have become sluggish: dull and slow to take in teaching, as they were not at first
decisions.reason: νωθροὶ means slow, dull, lazy. "You have become" implies that this was not always so (compare 10:32-34). The same adjective comes back in 6:12, so 5:11-6:12 is framed by it: here they are dull listeners, there the author hopes they will not become sluggish in hope.

decisions.choice: sluggish (Balanced), lazy (Readable)
decisions.reason: The same English word is used here and in 6:12 at each level, so the reader can see the frame the author builds.

records.heading: From milk to solid food

records.source: καὶ γὰρ ὀφείλοντες εἶναι διδάσκαλοι διὰ τὸν χρόνον, πάλιν χρείαν ἔχετε τοῦ διδάσκειν ὑμᾶς τινὰ τὰ στοιχεῖα τῆς ἀρχῆς τῶν λογίων τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ γεγόνατε χρείαν ἔχοντες γάλακτος, οὐ στερεᾶς τροφῆς.
records.gloss: Even for owing to be teachers because of the time, again need you have [of] the [one] to teach you someone the elements of the beginning of the oracles of the God, and you have become need having of milk, not of solid food.
pieces: Given the time that has passed, you ought to be teachers by now; yet once more you need someone to teach you the most basic elements of God's oracles. You have become people who need milk rather than solid food.

L.12: For indeed, though you ought to be teachers by reason of the time, again you have need of someone to teach you the elements of the beginning of the oracles of God, and you have become [people] having need of milk, not of solid food.

R.12: You have had enough time that you should be teaching others by now. But you need someone to teach you the ABCs of God's message all over again. You have become people who need milk, not solid food.

decisions.choice: someone: you need someone to teach you
alternatives: what: you need to be taught what the elements are
decisions.reason: Early manuscripts have no accents. The SBLGNT accents the word as τινὰ, the indefinite "someone", the subject of "to teach". Accented the other way it would be the question word "what", giving "you need someone to teach you what the elements are". The sense is nearly the same.

decisions.choice: the first elements of God's oracles: the most basic teaching of what God has spoken
alternatives: the first letters of the alphabet
decisions.reason: στοιχεῖα are the elements of a thing, such as the letters of the alphabet or the first principles of a subject; "of the beginning" makes the point stronger. "The oracles of God" are God's spoken words, the Scriptures (Romans 3:2; Acts 7:38), and here also the message about Christ built on them.

decisions.choice: milk and solid food: elementary teaching and mature teaching
decisions.reason: Milk is food for infants; solid food is for adults. The author uses the picture for the first teachings (listed in 6:1-2) and for fuller teaching, here the priesthood of Christ like Melchizedek's. Paul uses the same picture in 1 Corinthians 3:1-2. In 1 Peter 2:2 milk is a good picture for the word itself; the point here is not that milk is bad but that the readers should have outgrown living on it.

decisions.choice: the ABCs of God's message
alternatives: the basic principles of God's word
decisions.reason: "ABCs" gives the picture behind στοιχεῖα (the letters one learns first) in everyday words.

records.source: πᾶς γὰρ ὁ μετέχων γάλακτος ἄπειρος λόγου δικαιοσύνης, νήπιος γάρ ἐστιν·
records.gloss: Everyone for the [one] partaking of milk [is] inexperienced in word of righteousness, an infant for he is.
pieces: Whoever feeds on milk has no experience in the word of righteousness; that person is still an infant.

L.13: For everyone who partakes of milk [is] inexperienced in [the] word of righteousness, for [such a one] is an infant.

R.13: Anyone who is still drinking milk is a baby and has no experience with the teaching about righteousness.

decisions.choice: the word of righteousness: teaching about righteousness, the kind that trains a person to tell right from wrong
alternatives: ordinary adult speech, which an infant cannot follow
the message that God makes people righteous
decisions.reason: The phrase is unusual. It can mean the message about righteousness, mature teaching that shapes a person in what is right, which suits verse 14 (training to tell good from evil). Since "infant" can mean one who cannot yet speak, some take it as normal, correct speech. Others hear the message of how God makes people righteous. The translation keeps "word of righteousness" so all of these remain open.

decisions.choice: infant: a young child, the opposite of the mature in verse 14
decisions.reason: νήπιος is a little child. Deuteronomy 1:39 describes little children as those who do not yet know good from evil, the very thing the mature can do in verse 14.

decisions.choice: has no experience
decisions.reason: ἄπειρος means without experience or trial of something; "has no experience" says it simply and fits the picture of a child who has not yet learned.

records.source: τελείων δέ ἐστιν ἡ στερεὰ τροφή, τῶν διὰ τὴν ἕξιν τὰ αἰσθητήρια γεγυμνασμένα ἐχόντων πρὸς διάκρισιν καλοῦ τε καὶ κακοῦ.
records.gloss: Of perfect [ones] but is the solid food, of the [ones] through the practice the faculties trained having for distinguishing good both and evil.
pieces: Solid food, on the other hand, belongs to the mature, whose faculties have been trained by practice to tell good from evil.

L.14: But solid food is for [the] perfect, for those who through practice have [their] faculties trained for distinguishing both good and evil.

R.14: But solid food is for grown-ups. They have used their powers of judgment again and again and trained them to tell what is good from what is evil.

decisions.choice: perfect: mature, fully grown, as opposed to infants
decisions.reason: τελείων is from the same family as "made perfect" in 5:9 and "perfection" in 6:1. Set against "infant" in verse 13, it means a grown adult. The author chooses the word to link the readers' growth with the goal Christ has reached (5:9).

decisions.choice: faculties trained by practice: powers of perception exercised until they work by habit
decisions.reason: αἰσθητήρια are the senses or powers of perception. γεγυμνασμένα is the verb of athletic training (from it comes "gymnasium"); 12:11 uses it again for training by discipline. ἕξιν is a settled state reached by practice.

decisions.choice: to tell good from evil: moral discernment, the mark of an adult
alternatives: to tell good food from bad
decisions.reason: In the Old Testament, knowing good and evil marks the move from childhood to maturity (Deuteronomy 1:39; Isaiah 7:15-16). The food picture continues, but the point is the ability to judge what is right.

decisions.choice: mature (Balanced), grown-ups (Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "perfect" to show the link with 5:9 and 6:1. Balanced and Readable say "mature" and "grown-ups", because "perfect" set against "infant" would mislead.
